# Does your USB-C cable limit charging speed?

**Yes, it can.** Charging speed is set by the weakest of three parts: the charger, the device, and the cable. A 100W charger and a 100W laptop will still charge slowly through a cable that only supports 60W.

## What the tiers mean

| Cable rating | Electrical spec | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **60W** | 20V at 3A | Fine for phones, tablets, and most small laptops |
| **100W** | 20V at 5A, with an e-marker chip | Older tier (see below) |
| **240W** | 48V at 5A (Extended Power Range) | Needs an e-marker; the charger and device must also support 240W |

Sources: [UL Solutions](https://www.ul.com/insights/240w-usb-c-cable-performance-testing-and-safety-considerations), [USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/usb-charger-pd).

- **The 100W tier is no longer official.** USB-IF replaced 100W USB-C cables with 240W ones in its spec and stopped certifying 100W cables on December 22, 2021. Certified USB-C to USB-C cables are now labeled either 60W or 240W ([UL Solutions](https://www.ul.com/insights/240w-usb-c-cable-performance-testing-and-safety-considerations), [USB-IF Compliance Updates](https://compliance.usb.org/index.asp?Format=Standard&UpdateFile=Cables+and+Connectors&pubDate=20261005)). Plenty of 100W-rated cables are still sold, but they aren't an official tier.
- **A cable can't add power.** USB-IF notes that a certified cable doesn't augment the capabilities of the products it connects ([USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/cable_connector)). A 240W cable on a 65W charger still gives you 65W.
- **Higher voltage needs the right hardware.** The 28V, 36V, and 48V levels that enable 140W, 180W, and 240W only work when the charger, device, and e-marked cable all support them ([USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/usb-charger-pd)).

## How to check your cable

1. **Look for a 60W or 240W logo** on the cable or its packaging. USB-IF requires one on every certified USB-C to USB-C cable ([USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/cable_connector)).
2. **Check the specs or listing** for "5A" or "e-marked" if you need more than 60W.
3. **Search the USB-IF certified product list** at [usb.org/products](https://www.usb.org/products) if you want a verified cable.
4. **Be careful with unmarked cables.** If a cable has no rating, assume 60W or less.

## What to buy

- **Phone, tablet, or small laptop (up to about 60W):** any decent 60W cable is enough.
- **Laptop drawing 65-100W:** get a cable rated 5A or 240W.
- **Gaming laptop or anything above 100W:** you need a true 240W cable plus a charger that supports it.

One example is the [Baseus USB-C to USB-C 100W cable](https://dealectric.com/go/baseus-usb-c-cable-100w), listed at $9.99 for 1 m (the page shows 2 m at $12.99 and 3 m at $16.99, last verified 2026-10-21). It is rated 100W (5A, e-marked), but note its limits:
- It is not rated for 140W or 240W.
- It is USB 2.0 only (480 Mbps) with no video output.
- Baseus says it isn't supported for iPad Pro charging.
